summary: Discusses ways to improve the reliability of TIP and Tenex connections, covering obtaining and maintaining connections, recovery from lost connections, and connection-state changes.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes ways to keep TIP and TENEX connections understandable after a host or network interruption. The changes let hosts resynchronize connection state and tell users when service stops or resumes.

questions: how did early networks handle crashes
how did rfc 636 recover lost connections
what are the ras rar and rap commands
what is a half closed connection
subtitle: A plan for recovering TIP and TENEX connections after interruptions or lost messages.

tldr.problem: Lost messages, service interruptions, and host restarts could leave the two ends of a connection with inconsistent state or make a connection appear to hang up.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes host-availability notices, a reentrant TIP logger, allocation resynchronization commands, recovery after TENEX bughalts, and detection of half-closed connections.
tldr.outcome: The plan had been partly implemented in TIP and TENEX versions identified by the RFC and was undergoing final tests at publication.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 636 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. The RFC describes a reliability plan and reports that major portions were being tested.

sections.title: Connection Problems
sections.content: The authors focus on TIP and TENEX because many users relied on connections between them, while noting that the work could apply to other host types. The problems include hosts going down without explanation, login timeouts, lost allocations, system interruptions, and connections that one end thinks are closed while the other thinks they remain open.
sections.plainLanguage: After a failure, two computers can disagree about whether a connection is open or how much data may be sent. Users also need clear notices when a host becomes unavailable.

sections.title: Resynchronizing Allocation State
sections.content:
The RFC adds RAS (Reset Allocation by Sender), RAR (Reset Allocation by Receiver), and RAP (Reset Allocation Please). A sender can use RAS to request a reset; the receiver replies with RAR, and both sides set allocations to zero before normal transmission resumes.

RAP lets a receiver suggest that the sender resynchronize when it detects an unusual condition.
sections.plainLanguage: When the two sides lose track of their allocation state, the sender can request a reset. The reply confirms that both sides can start again from a known state.

sections.title: Interrupted and Half-Closed Connections
sections.content:
After a recoverable TENEX bughalt, the system can reinitialize its IMP interface and attempt to resynchronize allocations while keeping connections. The TIP reports that the host is not responding and later reports when service resumes; a full reload instead closes connections.

For half-closed connections, the RFC adds NXR and NXS responses and consistency checks so the still-open end can close its connection when the other end no longer has it.
sections.plainLanguage: Some interruptions can be followed by a connection recovery, while a full reload closes the connection. New checks help both sides agree when only one side still thinks a connection is open.
